question: What does Big-O notation actually describe, and why would you care about the difference between O(n) and O(n^2) in practice?
idealAnswer:
Big-O describes how the runtime (or space) of an algorithm grows as the input size grows, it's about growth rate, not exact runtime in seconds

It describes worst-case (or sometimes average-case) behavior as input size approaches large n, constant factors and small-input performance are intentionally ignored

Gives a correct concrete comparison: O(n) means work grows proportionally with input, O(n^2) means work grows with the square, e.g. a nested loop over the same list

Explains practical relevance: an O(n^2) algorithm that's fine on 100 items can become unusably slow on 1,000,000 items, which is why complexity matters for anything that scales

Bonus: mentions that Big-O ignores constants, so a technically 'worse' Big-O algorithm can still be faster in practice for small or bounded inputs
